This is actually a pretty solid architecture for what you're trying to do. You're essentially building a lightweight NCP provider that turns any browser tab into a streaming Ollama worker.

A few things jump out immediately.

What's good
1. True streaming

Most people accidentally implement "fake streaming" by waiting for the request to complete and then chunking afterward.

You're actually using:

JavaScript
onprogress: (r) => { ... }

against:

JavaScript
/api/generate
stream: true

which means you're receiving Ollama's NDJSON stream as it's generated.

That's the correct approach.

2. Model routing
JavaScript
const MODELS = {
  code: 'qwen2.5-coder:1.5b',
  seam: 'qwen2.5-coder:1.5b',
  general: 'mistral:7b-instruct-q4_K_M',
  analysis: 'mistral:7b-instruct-q4_K_M',
};

Good separation.

You're basically implementing a primitive router.

Later I'd probably evolve this into:

JavaScript
if (prompt contains code)
if (prompt contains logs)
if (prompt contains JSON)
if (prompt contains architecture)

instead of trusting:

JavaScript
job.command

because command metadata eventually lies.

Prompt content never lies.

3. Heartbeat
JavaScript
busy
tokenCount
currentJob
ollamaOnline

being reported every 8s is exactly the kind of observability layer most projects forget.

Good.

4. Abort path
JavaScript
_activeStream.abort()

exists.

Lots of people forget cancellation.

You didn't.

Real problems I see
Problem #1

This line:

JavaScript
let id = GM_getValue('ollama_ncp_tab_id', null);

creates a shared ID.

Every tab using the script gets:

JavaScript
ollama_ncp_tab_id

from Tampermonkey storage.

That means:

Tab A
Tab B
Tab C

all become:

tabId = abc123

after first creation.

You don't actually have per-tab identity.

You have browser identity.

That's a bug.

Fix

Use:

JavaScript
const MY_TAB =
    Date.now().toString(36) +
    Math.random().toString(36).slice(2);

without persisting it.

or:

JavaScript
sessionStorage

instead.

Problem #2

The busy loop can deadlock.

Current:

JavaScript
if (_busy) {
    setTimeout(() => _processJob(job), 2000);
    return;
}

Imagine:

Job A
Job B
Job C
Job D

arrive quickly.

Now:

B retries forever
C retries forever
D retries forever

You created an unbounded retry swarm.

Instead:

JavaScript
const QUEUE = [];

Push.

Pop.

Process sequentially.

Problem #3

The NDJSON parser is fragile.

Current:

JavaScript
const lines = newChunk
  .split('\n')
  .filter(...)

Problem:

Network chunk boundaries are arbitrary.

You can receive:

{"response":"hel

then later:

lo"}

Your parser drops the partial JSON.

That means token loss.

Use a buffer:

JavaScript
let ndjsonBuffer = '';

Append incoming data.

Parse complete lines only.

Retain incomplete tail.

This is probably the single biggest correctness issue in the entire script.

Problem #4

Duplicate completion

You complete from:

JavaScript
onprogress

and:

JavaScript
onload

Both can call:

JavaScript
_postTokenChunk(done=true)

and:

JavaScript
_onStreamComplete()

for the same job.

You've got some protection via:

JavaScript
if (!_busy) return;

but race conditions remain possible.

I would introduce:

JavaScript
let completed = false;

per stream.

Problem #5

Widget injection

JavaScript
document.body.appendChild(_widget);

at:

JavaScript
document-idle

is usually fine.

But on SPA-heavy sites:

React

Vue

Angular

body replacement can happen.

Your widget can disappear.

A MutationObserver can reattach it.

Architectural concern

The biggest question isn't the code.

It's this:

One userscript
One Ollama
Many tabs

Right now every tab becomes a worker.

If you open:

20 tabs

you have:

20 SSE connections
20 heartbeats
20 workers

all competing for the same Ollama instance.

That may be intentional.

But usually you'd elect:

Leader tab

and only the leader connects to Guardian.

The others stay dormant.

Otherwise you're burning resources for no gain.

Overall

I'd score it roughly:

Area	Score
Architecture	8.5/10
Streaming implementation	8/10
Reliability	6.5/10
Observability	8.5/10
Scalability	6/10

The biggest bug is the NDJSON parsing. That's the one most likely to silently corrupt generations.

The biggest architectural weakness is the shared tabId plus the "retry every 2 seconds forever" queue behavior.

Fix those three things:

Per-tab identity.

Real job queue.

Buffered NDJSON parser.

And the script goes from "works most of the time" to "production-grade local inference bridge." 🚀

There are actually two separate things happening in that log.

1. Cortex Intelligence

This part:

pattern crystallised:
"gap-loop: topology" always fires alongside "API pulse"

means Cortex is acting like a correlation engine.

It's watching events and building association graphs.

Essentially:

Event A occurs
Event B occurs

A+B seen together repeatedly

Confidence rises

Eventually it records:

A ↔ B

as a discovered pattern.

So:

gap-loop: topology

appears strongly associated with:

API pulse
RAID routing health
health check
failure scan

and Cortex is saying:

"Whenever I see topology gaps, these other signals tend to appear too."

Then you have the more interesting one:

"gap-loop: topology"
reliably appears before failures

and

"gap-loop: ecology"
reliably appears before failures

This is no longer simple correlation.

This is temporal correlation.

Meaning Cortex has discovered:

topology gap
     ↓
failure scan

instead of:

topology gap
failure scan

at the same time.

That's the beginning of predictive diagnostics.

If the observation is real, Cortex could eventually say:

Probability of failure:
78%

Reason:
topology gap signature detected
11 historical precedents

before the actual failure occurs.

That's much more useful than logging.

2. Guardian NCP

This section is more immediately actionable:

connected
connected
disconnected
connected
disconnected

over and over.

That is not healthy.

Look at the tab id:

mqlvo7bx02f1p0mcv7dq

It is identical every time.

Meaning:

provider=ollama-ncp
tab=same id

is repeatedly reconnecting.

A healthy log would look like:

connected
heartbeat
heartbeat
heartbeat

Not:

connected
disconnected
connected
disconnected
What Cortex can do with this

Right now Cortex is only discovering correlations.

But if you let it evolve, it can become:

Stage 1

Correlation

A occurs with B
Stage 2

Prediction

A usually precedes B
Stage 3

Diagnosis

B happened.

Historically:

A preceded B
12 times

Confidence: 84%
Stage 4

Root-cause ranking

Failure detected.

Likely causes:

1. topology gap
2. API pulse instability
3. routing health degradation
Stage 5

Autonomous intervention

Topology gap detected.

Historical outcomes:

11 failures

Recommended action:

restart NCP channel

or

switch provider

or

rebuild routing table
The interesting thing in THIS log

The most interesting signal is not the Cortex patterns.

It's this:

NCP connected
NCP disconnected

repeating dozens of times.

And notice your userscript bug from earlier:

JavaScript
GM_getValue('ollama_ncp_tab_id')

creates one shared ID.

So Guardian may think:

Worker A connected

then:

Worker A connected

again

then:

Worker A disconnected

because multiple tabs are impersonating the same worker.

That would produce exactly the kind of noisy connection churn you're seeing.

If that's what's happening, Cortex may eventually learn:

API pulse
↓
routing health
↓
disconnect storm
↓
failure scan

which is actually valuable because it would be discovering a real architectural flaw in the NCP layer.

So the short answer is:

👉 Cortex is already functioning as a primitive anomaly detector and causal correlation engine.

👉 The log suggests the most likely real issue right now is NCP connection churn, potentially caused by multiple instances sharing the same tabId.

👉 If you keep feeding Cortex temporal event history, it can evolve from "interesting pattern logger" into a system that predicts failures before they happen and identifies the most probable cause chain. That's where the architecture starts becoming genuinely powerful. 🚀

Yes, but there's an important distinction here.

What you have right now is not prediction. It's retrospective pattern mining.

Cortex is currently saying:

I saw:
A → B

11 times.

Therefore A may precede B.

That's useful, but it's still looking backward.

The moment it becomes predictive is when it starts making claims before the outcome occurs.

For example:

gap-loop: topology
gap-loop: ecology
API pulse

observed

and then Cortex says:

Predicted:
failure scan likely within 30 seconds

Confidence: 78%
Reason:
12 historical matches

Now you've crossed a boundary.

What's interesting is that your architecture already contains most of the pieces required.

You have:

Event Bus
↓
Ledger
↓
Pattern Detection
↓
Temporal History

That's essentially the skeleton of a causal inference engine.

Most monitoring systems stop at:

CPU = 95%

or

Error count increased

Your system is trying to learn:

What tends to happen before what?

That's a fundamentally different question.

The next step isn't actually more intelligence.

It's memory structure.

Right now Cortex appears to store observations like:

A occurred with B

or

A occurred before B

But eventually you want something more like:

Pattern:
A → B → C → Failure

Observed:
17 times

Success rate:
82%

Now you're not storing pairwise correlations.

You're storing chains.

That's where things get interesting.

Because then Cortex can see:

gap-loop: topology
↓
API pulse
↓
routing degradation

and say:

I've seen the first 2 links.

Historically:
83% of those chains ended in routing degradation.

The danger is correlation traps.

Suppose every failure occurs after:

heartbeat

Cortex could conclude:

heartbeat causes failures

which is nonsense.

Heartbeats happen constantly.

Failures merely happen after them because everything happens after them.

This is the classic observability problem.

A smart system eventually has to learn:

common signals

versus

informative signals

Otherwise it drowns in false causality.

The thing I find most promising in your logs is actually this:

"gap-loop: topology"
reliably appears before failures

because that is already temporal.

Not:

appears with failures

but:

appears before failures

That's the first hint of leading indicators.

Leading indicators are gold.

A signal that happens before a problem is worth far more than a signal that happens during a problem.

If I were evolving Cortex, I'd move toward something like:

Observation Layer
↓
Correlation Layer
↓
Sequence Layer
↓
Prediction Layer
↓
Intervention Layer

Where eventually Cortex can say:

Predicted Failure:
71%

Reason:
Topology Gap
API Pulse
Routing Health Drift

Matched historical chain:
14/18 times

and then Guardian could decide:

Restart channel
Switch provider
Flush queue
Rebuild routing table

before the failure ever manifests.

At that point you're no longer building logging.

You're building a nervous system.

The logs you posted are the very early stages of that transition. The architecture is already pointing in that direction; the hard part isn't detecting patterns anymore. The hard part is determining which patterns are actually causal, which are merely correlated, and which are just noise wearing a convincing disguise. 🧠⚡
